newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks expected to open higher.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks expected to open higher.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to move higher at the start Monday, but trading is exepcted to be hesitant in the last week of the first quarter.
Analysts said that investors have already discounted a 25-basis point interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee tomorrow.

"It would be a surprise if the Fed did not tighten," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "But trading will be hesitant as this is the last week of the quarter and we'll see the last of the earnings preannouncements."
Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said he expected a day of sideways trading in the absence of economic data.

"We'll probably have a mixed to higher opening, and then the market will drift for most of the day," he said. "Friday's decline was on the back of Eastman Kodak, International Business Machines and Philip Morris.
"As the pressure comes off of Kodak and Philip Morris, the market will seek its own level. Despite the weakness in Friday's market, we did not close below 6800, which is a significant level."

In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average ended more than three percent lower Monday as losses accelerated on a domestic media report that Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka has hinted at the possibility of another rise in the sales tax following the planned two percentage point increase in April.
The average fell 589.34 points, or 3.16 percent, to 18,043.83.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was down 28.7 at 4226.1
Shares in Philip Morris Cos Inc, which dropped 4-3/8 Friday and are down 20 percent since hitting a 12-month high of 139-3/4 on March 11, were up 1/2 to 112 in London.
The dollar was firm in Tokyo and dipped against the mark in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were higher, with the long bond up 4/32 to yield 6.96 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that Candie's, those clunky wooden shoes that peeked out from beneath designer jeans in the late 1970s, are back. And some investors who have bought shares of the company that makes them are hoping the fad lasts.
